title: Shweta Agarwal vs Neeraj Saini on 10 June, 2026
full_text: Shweta Agarwal vs Neeraj Saini on 10 June, 2026 IN THE COURT OF Ms. AASTHA SHARMA, LD. JMFC (N.I. Act)-03, SOUTH-EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURTS COMPLEX: DELHI Shweta Agarwal Vs. No. 126A, Hari Nagar, Ashram, New Delhi - 110014. AASTHA SHARMA CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 1 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:04:50 +0530 3. Name of the accused person(s), parentage Sh. Neeraj Saini & residential address S/o Sh. Bal Kishan Saini, R/o 227, Hari Nagar, Ashram, New Delhi-110014. 4. Offence complained of or proved U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 5. Plea of the accused Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6. Final Judgment/order Acquittal 7. Date of judgment/order 10.06.2026 Date of Institution : 21.03.2016 Date of Reserving Judgment/Order : 06.06.2026 Date of Pronouncement of Judgment/Order : 10.06.2026 ARGUING COUNSELS: Ld. Counsel for the complainant : Ms. Suhani Gupta Ld. Counsel for the Accused : Sh.Uday Shankar Pandey CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 2 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:04:57 +0530 JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant Ms. Shweta Agarwal (hereinafter referred to as "complainant") against Sh. Neeraj Saini (hereinafter referred to as the "accused") under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, the complainant is working as an interior designer and is a neighbour of the accused and had friendly relations with the accused. That, in the month of June 2025, the accused approached the complainant at her residence and requested for a friendly loan of Rs. 20,00,000/- for a period of 6-7 months for her business expansion needs. That, in pursuance of the same, the complainant advanced Rs. 14 lakhs in cash to the accused on 15.06.2015 as a friendly loan and in discharge of the said loan, the accused issued a post dated cheque bearing no. 562779 dated 15.01.2016 in the sum of Rs. 14,00,000/- drawn on Punjab National Bank, Maharani Bagh, New Delhi in favour of the complainant with the assurance that the same shall be honoured upon presentation on due date. That, a written agreement dated 15.06.2015 to this effect was also entered between the complainant and the accused. That, upon assurance and representation of accused no. 1, the complainant presented the said cheque before her bank Punjab National Bank, Maharani Bagh, New Delhi, however, the same was returned unpaid with remarks "Funds Insufficient" vide return memo dated 22.01.2016. CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 3 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:05:04 +0530 B. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused person through his counsel, dated 08.02.2016, thereby requiring the accused person to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheques within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the accused person through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at their correct address. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the Accused person has deliberately and willfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused persons, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the complainant examined himself on affidavit being Ex. CW1/A and relied on documents Ex. CW1/1 to Ex. CW1/6 and Ex. CW1/X. 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused was summoned. 5. Upon the appearance of the accused, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon him on 25.01.2020 to which he pleaded not guilty. The accused has stated that he had given the cheque in question to the mother of the complainant for the purpose of committee and that he does not owe any liability towards the complainant. CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 4 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:05:09 +0530 6. CW-1 was examined-in-chief, cross-examined and discharged. Thereby, CE was closed on 28.06.2023. Accordingly, matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused. 7. Statement of accused under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 CrPC was recorded on 27.01.2024 wherein the accused opted to lead defence evidence. However, despite several opportunities being granted to the accused, he failed to lead DE and therefore vide order of this court, DE was closed on 05.06.2024. 8. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After hearing the final arguments from both sides, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. 9. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 5 of 15 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:05:14 +0530 IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. 10. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: I. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 6 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:05:20 +0530 order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: 11. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheque, i.e., bearing no. 562779 dated 15.01.2016 for Rs. 14,00,000/- drawn on Punjab National Bank, Maharani Bagh, New Delhi (Ex. CW1/1). In notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused has admitted that the cheque in dispute belongs to him. It is also not disputed that the cheque in question is not drawn on the account maintained by the accused and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused is the drawer of the cheque. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 12. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 7 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:05:25 +0530 drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheque in question was returned vide return memo dated 22.01.2016 (Ex. CW1/2) due to the reason "Funds Insufficient." By implication thereof, the cheque was presented within three months and the same was returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 13. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 08.02.2016 (Ex. CW1/3) was dispatched on 08.02.2016 vide Speed Post (Ex. CW1/4 & Ex. CW1/5), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheques in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused has not admitted to the receiving of legal demand notice in notice u/s 251 CrPC. However, as per the presumption raised under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand notice is sent at the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by virtue of giving of legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. 14. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 8 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:05:31 +0530 Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act 15. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." 16. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 9 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:06:01 +0530 (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 17. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheques and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? 18. In the present case, in order to discharge her initial burden to prove the abovementioned ingredients, the complainant relied upon the affidavit of the complainant being Ex. CW1/A and placed on record documents mentioned hereinbefore. The case of the complainant is that the accused had borrowed a sum of Rs. 14,00,000/- from the complainant for business purposes and the cheque in question was issued in pursuance of the same. The primary defence of the accused is that the cheque in question was handed over to the mother of the complainant for the purpose of a committee and the accused has already paid the sum to the complainant and no loan was ever advanced by the complainant to the accused. CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 10 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:06:06 +0530 19. The complainant has placed on record the loan agreement dated 15.06.2015 executed between the parties Ex. CW1/X which was placed on record at the stage of final arguments. The agreement is notarised and is attested by witnesses, however, no witness has been examined by the complainant in complainant evidence. The accused has denied the execution of the agreement and the complainant has also brought nothing on record to indicate to corroborate the authenticity of the contents of the agreement. Furthermore, the complainant in her cross-examination dated 21.12.2022 stated as follows: "...In the year 2015, my yearly income was approximately Rs. 10 lacs. I used to file ITR in the year 2015. I can bring the same if needed..." "..Rs. 5 lacs I had received from my maternal grand mother, some money I had arranged from gold loan and rest I had with me in cash. I can bring the documents regarding the gold loan on next date of hearing.." On the next date of hearing, the complainant in her CW-1 dated 25.01.2023 has stated that she could not trace out the documents regarding the gold loan taken and has admitted that as per her ITR, her gross income is Rs. 3,09,586/-. The complainant has further stated as follows: "...It is correct that I had not mentioned in my legal notice, my complaint and my evidence that I had received Rs. 5,00,000/- as a gift from my maternal grandmother. I do not have any documentary proof which could show that my maternal CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 11 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.06.10 16:06:12 +0530 grandmother had given Rs. 5,00,000/- as a gift. (Vol. It was given in cash). I did not deposit this amount of Rs. 5 lacs in any bank...." "...I do not remember how much money was there in my bank account in the year 2015 in the month of June but I can place on record my bank account statement.." On the next date of hearing, the complainant as CW-1 in her examination dated 28.06.2023 has stated that she was unable to bring her bank statement before the court. Therefore, the complainant has been unable to furnish any proof for her financial capacity, vis-a-vis receipt for payment received from her grandmother, relevant documents for the gold loan procured, relevant withdrawal receipt or bank account statement to indicate that the loan was advanced by the complainant to the accused. 20. At this stage, it would be relevant to refer to the decision of the Hon'ble High court of Delhi in the case titled as Sheela Sharma vs. Mahender Pal (2016 SCC Online Del 4696), where inter-alia, it was observed that: "31. In cases where the complainant claims to have advanced a friendly loan in cash, and where the transaction of loan is not evidenced by any other documentary or other reliable evidence, no doubt, the aspect whether the availability of funds in cash with the complainant/lender, and its advancement as loan to the accused have been reflected in Page no.14 of 17 Madan Khurana vs. Pankaj CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 12 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:06:24 +0530 Sharma CC No. 2233-2016 the income tax returns of the complainant/lender, or not, become relevant. If, the availability of funds, and the loan transaction itself is not so reflected, that factor is taken note of by the Court as relevant to hold that the presumption under Section 118 and 139 of the NI Act stands rebutted. However, these considerations would not be relevant, where loan transaction itself is otherwise established, either through documentary evidence-such as, a receipt or a loan agreement, or acknowledgement executed by the accused, or by oral evidence of an independent witness who is found to be credible. In the present case, the loan transaction, though not recorded in an agreement, or a receipt or acknowledgement executed by the accused, and though not reflected in the income-tax returns of the complainant, is evidenced by the oral testimony of CW-2, who is an independent witness and highly credible." Therefore, in cases in which the impugned loan transaction is in cash, the accused can raise a probable defence by questioning the financial capacity of the complainant, and once the said question is raised, the onus shifts on the complainant to prove his financial capacity. In the present case, admittedly, no documents were placed on record to show that the complainant was having sufficient funds with her to advance such a huge sum of money. Further, such a huge sum was provided by the complainant to the accused by taking out of her savings and by borrowing from her maternal grand mother and taking a gold loan, CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 13 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.06.10 16:06:31 +0530 without any security from the accused, which cannot be equated with the conduct of a prudent woman acting in similar circumstances. Furthermore, the agreement placed on record by the complainant is also not corroborated by examination of any witness to the agreement, and since the accused has denied the execution of the agreement, it raises suspicion on the authenticity of the agreement Ex. CW1/X. 21. In view of the aforesaid findings and analysis, this court has arrived at an irresistible conclusion that the accused has been able to cast a shadow of reasonable doubt upon the case of the complainant by rebutting the mandatory presumption resting in its favour and by several inconsistencies in the version of the complainant. Once the accused had created a probable defence as to the legally enforceable liability, the onus shifted on the complainant to prove the existence of legally enforceable liability of the accused, as on the date of the drawal or presentation of the impugned cheques, which has not been fulfilled by the complainant in the present case. Since this basic ingredient which is pivotal to attract liability under Section 138 NI Act has not been proved by the complainant, accordingly, no offence of dishonour of the impugned cheque under the said Section is made out. 22. In light of the discussion above, ingredient no. II has not been fulfilled in the present case. Conclusion: 23. In view of the aforesaid discussion, the accused Neeraj Saini has been successful in establishing a probable defence on a standard of preponderance of probabilities to rebut the presumption under Section 118 and 139 of the NI Act by CC No. 632073/2016 Shweta Agarwal Vs. Neeraj Saini Page 14 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.06.10 16:06:39 +0530 punching holes in the case of the complainant and making the case of the complainant doubtful. The accused has been successful in establishing a probable defence and as a consequence, questioning the existence of legally enforceable liability in favour of the complainant and that the cheque was not issued by accused in discharge of existing legally enforceable debt or liability owed to the complainant. In the result of the analysis of the present case, the accused Neeraj Saini is hereby acquitted of the offence punishable under Section 138 , Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
